findings.finding: The `pre_materialization_pack_guard` AC states it 'rejects an unfiltered all-history pack above 131072 KiB and accepts blobless below 102400 KiB,' but the Production guardrails section assigns these two limits to different jobs and lifecycle phases: 102400 KiB is the standalone verify-identity checkout limit (before any tickets worktree exists) and 131072 KiB is the Gerrit post-materialization limit. A test named 'pre_materialization' that uses 131072 KiB as its rejection threshold contradicts the guardrails section, which reserves 131072 KiB for a post-materialization context. An implementer reading both sections will be uncertain which guard the integration test is exercising and whether the fixture correctly represents the standalone (102400 KiB) pre-materialization scenario or the Gerrit (131072 KiB) post-materialization scenario.
findings.location: Production guardrails section vs. AC `pre_materialization_pack_guard` / tests/integration/test_ci_tickets_partial_clone.py
scenarios: An implementer writes the integration test using 131072 KiB as the standalone guard threshold, incorrectly loosening the production check by 28 672 KiB.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the Git packet-capture mechanism (e.g. `GIT_TRACE_PACKET=/path/to/trace.log` passed in the subprocess env, then parsed from that file) so the capability/request regex assertions in the three direct/named-origin protocol-oracle tests are implementable.
evidence: Plan quotes: 'Require both: a server capability packet advertising filter, and a client-to-server packet matching packet: followed by any non-space actor ending in >, then exact content filter blob:none'
Plan quotes: 'Capture packet traces for plain named-origin inheritance, direct URL with --depth=1 --filter=blob:none, and direct URL full-history with --filter=blob:none'
ABSENCE: The plan never mentions GIT_TRACE_PACKET, GIT_TRACE2, or any other git environment variable that enables protocol-level packet logging.
ABSENCE: No file or section in the repo sets GIT_TRACE_PACKET (confirmed by search_files across the entire repo).

The probe format 'packet: fetch> filter blob:none' is characteristic of GIT_TRACE_PACKET output, but that variable must be set in the subprocess environment for git to emit it — the plan provides no instruction to do so.
findings.finding: The plan requires tests to assert a 'capability packet advertising filter' and a 'client-to-server packet matching packet: followed by any non-space actor ending in >, then exact content filter blob:none', but nowhere names the Git mechanism that produces protocol-level packet traces. The standard mechanism is the `GIT_TRACE_PACKET` environment variable (or `GIT_TRACE2` event log). Without specifying how to capture these packets, the three protocol-oracle ACs (`named_origin_filter`, `direct_depth_filter`, `direct_full_filter`) and their capability/request regex assertions cannot be implemented by an executor — they have no signal to parse.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle section: 'Capture packet traces for plain named-origin inheritance, direct URL with --depth=1 --filter=blob:none, and direct URL full-history with --filter=blob:none. Each must satisfy the capability/request regex and missing-blob oracle.' Also AC lines for named_origin_filter, direct_depth_filter, direct_full_filter.
scenarios: An executor implementing the integration test sets up the git daemon correctly but has no way to obtain packet-level output to match the capability/request regex, causing all three protocol-oracle ACs to be unimplementable as written.

An executor guesses GIT_TRACE_PACKET but sets it to '1' (integer form, which git ignores — GIT_TRACE_PACKET requires a file path or fd number or the literal 'true'/'1' is actually accepted in recent git), potentially producing no output and silent test failures.
findings.suggested_fix: In the 'Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle' section, add: 'Set `GIT_TRACE_PACKET=<tmpfile>` in the environment of the `git fetch`/`git clone` subprocess; after the call, read `<tmpfile>` and apply the capability/request regex. Each trace file is per-invocation to avoid cross-test contamination.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define an explicit teardown/retirement protocol for the git daemon subprocess (e.g., a pytest fixture with `yield` + `process.terminate()`/`process.wait()` in finally, scoped at session or module level) so the bound port and process are always released, even on test failure.
evidence: Plan text: 'Start git daemon as a localhost subprocess with --export-all and --enable=upload-pack.'
Plan text: 'Reserve a loopback port and poll the socket with a bounded deadline.'
ABSENCE: No teardown, fixture finalization, context-manager, or atexit cleanup is specified anywhere in the plan for the daemon process or its port.

The daemon is consumed by at least three test cases (named_origin_filter, direct_depth_filter, direct_full_filter, reconverges, pre/post_materialization_pack_guard) across two test files; any one failure leaves the resource live.
findings.finding: The git daemon subprocess — a shared mutable resource (bound TCP port + running process) created by the test fixture — has no defined retirement or teardown path. The plan specifies creation ('Start git daemon as a localhost subprocess') and liveness detection ('poll the socket with a bounded deadline') but says nothing about fixture finalization, cleanup on test failure, or daemon shutdown. On long-lived CI runners or when an integration test fails mid-run, the daemon process persists and its port remains bound, causing subsequent pytest invocations to fail with EADDRINUSE and leaving zombie daemon processes accumulating across runs.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle section — 'Start git daemon as a localhost subprocess … Reserve a loopback port and poll the socket with a bounded deadline.'
scenarios: CI runner reuse (e.g., GitHub Actions self-hosted runner or any long-lived runner): a failing test leaves the daemon running; the next pytest invocation on the same runner finds the port already bound and the daemon fixture fails to start, breaking the entire integration test suite.
Parallel pytest-xdist execution: two worker processes each try to start a daemon, one wins the port and the other sees EADDRINUSE with no retry or fallback specified.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap daemon startup in a pytest `session`-scoped fixture using `yield`: start the daemon, yield the (host, port) tuple, then unconditionally call `process.terminate(); process.wait(timeout=5)` in the finally block. Bind an ephemeral OS-assigned port by passing `--port=0` if supported, or by letting the OS assign one via `socket.bind(('127.0.0.1', 0))` before passing the chosen port to the daemon, eliminating the reservation window.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Eliminate the port-reservation TOCTOU by using an OS-assigned ephemeral port: bind a Python socket to port 0, read back the assigned port, close the socket with SO_REUSEPORT set, and pass that exact port to git daemon — or document an alternative atomic hand-off strategy.
evidence: Plan text: 'Reserve a loopback port and poll the socket with a bounded deadline.'
Standard POSIX/TCP behavior: port availability check (bind-then-close) followed by a separate daemon invocation is non-atomic; the port is unbound between the check and daemon startup.
No plan text describes atomic port hand-off (e.g., SO_REUSEPORT, pre-binding a socket and passing the fd to the daemon, or OS-assigned ephemeral port selection).
findings.finding: The plan specifies 'Reserve a loopback port' then start the git daemon — a classic check-then-act TOCTOU race. Between the moment the plan probes a port for availability and the moment git daemon binds it, another process (another test worker, an unrelated OS service, or a concurrent CI job on a shared runner) can claim the same port. This is not an atomic operation and git daemon provides no mechanism to inherit an already-bound socket.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle section — 'Reserve a loopback port and poll the socket with a bounded deadline.'
scenarios: Concurrent CI jobs on a shared or matrix runner: two jobs each probe overlapping port ranges and collide, causing one daemon to fail to bind and the corresponding integration tests to be silently skipped or error with a confusing connection-refused message.

Heavily loaded developer workstation (macOS or Linux): an ephemeral port chosen during the check step is grabbed by a local service before git daemon starts, producing a non-deterministic EADDRINUSE that is hard to reproduce.

findings.finding: The no-promisor guard design snapshots exact `git count-objects -v` output before and after `rebar verify-identity` and fails on any line difference, but Git's auto-gc/auto-pack (triggered by accumulation of loose objects from the materialization step or by internal gc.auto heuristics) can fire between the two snapshots and change pack-count or loose-count even when verify-identity adds zero objects, causing spurious CI failures.

evidence: Plan: 'snapshot exact git count-objects -v after materialization, run rebar verify-identity, snapshot again, and fail if any line differs'
ADR 0051 / bug 88eb / src/rebar/_commands/init.py: gc.autoDetach=false keeps auto-gc ENABLED foreground, only prevents detachment
tests/interfaces/store/test_gc_config.py: 'auto-gc stays ENABLED (loose growth is still bounded)' — gc.auto is UNSET so the default 6700-object threshold governs
worktree materialization fetches tip blobs (plan: 'Materialization may fetch tip blobs'), depositing loose objects that can cross the gc.auto threshold mid-sequence
findings.finding: The no-promisor guard mechanism — snapshot exact `git count-objects -v` before and after `rebar verify-identity`, fail on any line difference — will spuriously fail when auto-gc fires foreground between the two snapshots. The codebase explicitly keeps auto-gc ENABLED (gc.autoDetach=false per ADR 0051 / bug 88eb) so that repack bounds loose-object growth; the worktree materialization step deposits blob objects that can push the loose-object count above gc.auto's default 6700-object threshold. When gc fires foreground during the verify-identity invocation, it moves loose objects into a new pack file and changes both `count` and `size-pack` lines even though verify-identity itself added zero new objects. The before/after diff then flags a false promisor leak. This defeats the guard's purpose — a spuriously failing guard will be disabled or ignored.
findings.location: Production guardrails section: 'snapshot exact git count-objects -v after materialization, run rebar verify-identity, snapshot again, and fail if any line differs'; AC: standalone_no_promisor / gerrit_no_promisor / standalone_identity_no_promisor / gerrit_identity_no_promisor
scenarios: Materialization fetches ~N loose blob objects for the tickets tip; N crosses gc.auto=6700 default; git auto-gc fires foreground during the verify-identity invocation; loose objects are repacked; count-objects before shows M loose+0 packs, after shows 0 loose+1 pack; guard fails spuriously with no promisor leak.
On a slow CI runner the two snapshots bracket a background maintenance run triggered by an unrelated process, changing size-pack; guard fails.
findings.suggested_fix: Before taking the first snapshot, run `git -C <worktree> config gc.auto 0` (or export `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=gc.auto GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=0`) to suppress auto-gc for the duration of the before/after measurement. Restore with `git config --unset gc.auto` afterward. This keeps the mechanism logically correct while removing the auto-gc race.

findings.finding: The plan specifies the git-daemon test fixture serves a 'bare repo configured uploadpack.allowFilter=true', but `uploadpack.allowFilter` set at the repository level is silently ignored by git-daemon as a security measure — it must be set at global config scope or injected into the daemon via `--git-config uploadpack.allowFilter=true`. If the integration test sets this config only in the repo's `.git/config`, the daemon will silently drop all filters without error (falling back to full fetches and warning 'filtering not recognized by server, ignoring'), causing the `blob:none` contrast test to produce false-positive results (both filtered and unfiltered paths fetch the same large packfile).
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and safety section: 'serve a bare repo configured uploadpack.allowFilter=true'
findings.suggested_fix: In the fixture setup, pass the config to the daemon directly: `git daemon --git-config uploadpack.allowFilter=true --export-all ...` or write a temporary global gitconfig pointing `$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` at it. Assert in the test that `git ls-remote --filter=blob:none git://localhost:PORT/repo` receives a capability advertisement containing 'filter' before running the size-contrast assertions.

findings.finding: The integration fixture specifies 'serve a bare repo configured uploadpack.allowFilter=true', but git-daemon silently ignores uploadpack.allowFilter when set in a repository's local .git/config as a security measure — the option must be supplied to the daemon process via '--git-config uploadpack.allowFilter=true' on the daemon command line (or in the global git config). If the fixture sets this only in the bare repo's local config, the daemon serves without filter capability, and both the filtered and unfiltered fetch paths receive the full packfile, making the size-contrast threshold assertions pass vacuously regardless of whether blob:none is honored.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and safety section: 'Integration tests start git daemon as a localhost subprocess with --export-all and --enable=upload-pack, serve a bare repo configured uploadpack.allowFilter=true'
findings.suggested_fix: In the fixture, start git daemon as: `git daemon --reuseaddr --base-path=<dir> --export-all --enable=upload-pack --git-config=uploadpack.allowFilter=true git://<path>` — this injects the setting into the daemon process scope rather than the per-repo config that daemon ignores.

findings.finding: The plan mandates that integration tests assert `GIT_TRACE_PACKET` output contains the exact string `fetch> filter blob:none` to prove the filter was sent on the wire. However, the documented format for GIT_TRACE_PACKET output uses a `packet: git>` prefix (for client-sent lines) rather than `fetch>`, and protocol v2 fetch-pack writes the filter as a bare `filter <spec>` packet line. The exact string `fetch> filter blob:none` does not appear in any public Git documentation or test suite and is likely the wrong assertion pattern — tests checking for it may silently pass or fail depending on the Git version and protocol negotiated, and will be brittle across Git releases.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and safety section: 'Each trace must contain fetch> filter blob:none'
